title: Paneer Costs Seven Times More Per Gram of Protein Than Masoor Dal
excerpt: With paneer and pulse prices climbing, ThePrint argues India must grow far more protein — while households can stretch their protein rupee by leaning on cheaper dals.
body:
• ThePrint's Economix analysis: paneer costs nearly twice as much as chicken and fish — and nearly seven times more per gram of protein than masoor dal — the costliest protein for vegetarian households.
  • More than 70 per cent of Indians fail to meet their daily protein requirements; Indian diets run 60 to 70 per cent carbohydrates.
  • The government launched an Rs 11,440-crore Mission for Atmanirbharta in pulses (FY26–FY31), targeting 35 million tonnes of production by FY31, after imports hit a record $5.5 billion in FY25.
  • Reuters reported the government is weighing cuts to pulse import duties after a weak monsoon raised concerns over domestic crop production and food inflation.

The protein hierarchy

For vegetarian households, paneer sits at the top of the protein hierarchy — and of the price list too. In its Economix analysis, ThePrint's consulting editor for economics Bidisha Bhattacharya broke down the economics of protein inflation: paneer costs nearly twice as much as chicken and fish, and for families that abstain from eggs or meat, dairy is the primary protein source beyond dal. The starkest number: paneer costs nearly seven times more per gram of protein than masoor dal.

That matters because protein is the nutrient India is shortest of. National nutrition surveys indicate more than 70 per cent of Indians fail to meet daily protein requirements, and the Indian diet runs 60 to 70 per cent carbohydrates — white rice, refined flour, potatoes. The fallout runs from unstable blood sugar and continual hunger to slower metabolism and muscle loss.

Food inflation has shifted to protein

The finance ministry's Monthly Economic Report for August 2026 noted that food inflation is shifting in composition, with protein-rich items, processed foods and edible oils the major contributors to price pressures. Consumer Food Price Index inflation rose to 5.52 per cent in July 2026 from 5.32 per cent in June, with milk, chicken, mutton, fish, onion and arhar/tur recording notable inflation.

Why pulses lost favour

India is the world's largest producer and consumer of pulses — yet its pulse import bill grew more than three-fold, from $1.6 billion in FY21 to a record $5.5 billion in FY25. Mint's explainer traces the disconnect to the farm: pulses are low-productivity crops grown on marginal, rain-fed land. And while the government declares minimum support prices, assured purchases have been low — summer-grown moong, tur and urad were recently selling at 14 to 28 per cent discounts to MSP, because imports at very low or zero duties undercut domestic growers. Yellow peas imported from Canada at zero duty sell for under Rs 3,000 per quintal, against the government's MSP of Rs 5,875.

Productivity tells the deeper story. A Niti Aayog report put average pulse productivity at 740 kg per hectare — far below the global average of 949 kg and the 1,800-plus kg yields of Canada and the USA. Unlike cereals, pulses saw limited yield improvement for want of high-yielding varieties, and being rain-fed, yields are highly vulnerable to climate: of 27 recorded El Nino years between 1951 and 2024, fifteen saw declines in both pulse production and acreage. The irony is that pulses are more climate-friendly than cereals — they use less water and fix nitrogen in the soil, and an Arvind Subramanian committee calculation put the net social benefit of growing tur instead of rice at over Rs 13,000 per hectare — yet farmers still choose rice for its higher yields and better prices.

The policy push

The government's answer is the Mission for Atmanirbharta in pulses: Rs 11,440 crore over six years, FY26 to FY31, approved by the Cabinet on October 1. The mission will develop pest-resistant, climate-resilient varieties, bring 3.5 million more hectares under pulses, subsidise processing and post-harvest infrastructure, and assure purchase at MSP. Targets: 35 million tonnes of production by FY31, up from 25 million tonnes in FY25.

Reuters reported the government is considering cutting import duties on pulses after a weak monsoon. Meanwhile a major processor has authorised a Rs 100-crore programme to quadruple paneer capacity from 20 to 80 metric tonnes a day by June 2027, citing double-digit annual volume growth in retail paneer.

What it means for the plate

The policy push will take years to change what is grown; the immediate fix is on the plate, where households should lean on the cheapest protein they already have. A bowl of dal a day, curd with meals, and where acceptable, eggs or lean meat — the Indian kitchen does not need imported powders or expensive foods, only better choices from foods it already cooks. For the diaspora's largely vegetarian households, the same math holds: dal and pulses stretch the protein budget farthest, and until India grows enough of them, the prices of paneer and pulses are likely to keep climbing.
